metadata.title: On the generation of stable Kerr frequency combs in the Lugiato-Lefever model of periodic optical waveguides

extraction_notes.note: The proof of Theorem 2 is the whole of Section 4, spread over five subsections; it is split into one proof node per subsection (each with a proves edge to TP2 and a uses edge to the first part PP9). The Section 4 preamble (linearization, mu, W, M_h) is extracted as definitions rather than as a proof part.
Section 3.1 is an explicitly informal formal-expansion analysis. It is one heuristic remark, not a proof part of Theorem 1, whose rigorous proof (PP8) is Section 3.2 alone.

The paper reuses symbols: in Section 3.1 phi_h and sigma_h denote the near-zero eigenpair of tilde L, not the alpha=0 waves of DP6. In Appendix B, alpha is the dn amplitude and L_+ is written with 2phi_0^2. No DP6 edge to RP5 was added for that reason.

The signs in (B.1) and (B.4) rest on a Mathematica evaluation and on plotted functions (Figures 1 and 2) that are not in the source. The plot-based steps are kept inside the proof, and no rigor field is set on PrP7.

Appendix A is a derivation that ends with 'All this means is that...'. That sentence is taken as a claim (ClP9) and the derivation before it as its proof. The comments in between ('Our analysis is not precise enough...') and after it are left outside both nodes.
The numbered equation (3.25) 'D_1^0=0' is too short for the finishing step to match it to its environment, so its label 340 was set by hand and the \eqref{340} edge was added manually.

Literature discussion in the Introduction, the remarks on the practical uselessness of small solutions, and the comment that c must lie in (0,1/4) within O(h) for small h are left as text without nodes.

nodes.name: Informal analysis of the profile equation
nodes.statement: As we have mentioned above, we shall use $h$ as a small parameter, by taking $\alpha:=\alpha_0 h, \alpha_0=O(1)$. Next, we assume that \eqref{151} (or equivalently \eqref{160}) has a solution. In addition, we model $\tilde{{\mathcal L}}$ to be a small perturbation of ${\mathcal L}_{-,0}$. In particular, it has a small (and simple) eigenvalue close to zero (in order to produce $O(1)$ solutions of \eqref{160}), denoted by $\sigma_h=\sigma_0 h+O(h^2)$, with a corresponding eigenfunction $\varphi_h=\varphi_0+O(h)$. In addition, the next eigenvalue is positive and order $O(1)$. By projecting \eqref{160} onto $\varphi_h$ and its complementary subspace $\{\varphi_h\}^\perp$, we arrive at the formula \begin{eqnarray} \varphi_{\alpha,1} &=& \f{h \sigma}{\sigma^2+\alpha^2} \f{\dpr{1}{\varphi_h}}{\|\varphi_h\|^2} \varphi_h+q_1, \ \ q_1=O(h), q_1 \in \{\varphi_h\}^\perp \\ \varphi_{\alpha,2} &=& \f{\alpha h}{\sigma^2+\alpha^2} \f{\dpr{1}{\varphi_h}}{\|\varphi_h\|^2} \varphi_h+q_2, \ \ q_2=O(h^2), q_2 \in \{\varphi_h\}^\perp \end{eqnarray} One can in principle continue with the construction of $\varphi_{\alpha,1}, \varphi_{\alpha,2}$ based on \eqref{165} and \eqref{167}, but it becomes hard to keep track of the expansion of $\sigma_h$ in powers of $h$. Instead, we will pass to the known waves $\varphi_0$, since we have a good understanding of the operator ${\mathcal L}_{-,0}$, which we denote by $L_{-}$ henceforth\footnote{Also, we introduce $L_+:={\mathcal L}_{+,0}$}. More precisely, we postulate the form \begin{eqnarray} \varphi_{\alpha,1} &=& (a_0+a_1 h+O(h^2))\varphi_0+ h \Psi_1, \ \ \Psi_1\perp \varphi_0 \\ \varphi_{\alpha,2} &=& (b_0+b_1 h+O(h^2))\varphi_0+ h \Psi_2, \ \ \Psi_2\perp \varphi_0 \end{eqnarray} Comparing the expansions \eqref{165} with \eqref{170}(and \eqref{167} with \eqref{175} respectively), we have the formula \begin{eqnarray} a_0 &=& \f{\sigma_0}{\sigma_0^2+\alpha_0^2} \f{\dpr{1}{\varphi_0}}{\|\varphi_0\|^2} \\ b_0 &=& \f{\alpha_0}{\sigma_0^2+\alpha_0^2} \f{\dpr{1}{\varphi_0}}{\|\varphi_0\|^2} \end{eqnarray} Next, using the form of the operator $\tilde{{\mathcal L}}$, we have $$ \tilde{{\mathcal L}}=-\partial_x^2+1 - 2(\varphi_{\alpha,1}^2+\varphi_{\alpha,2}^2)= -\partial_x^2+1 - 2(a_0^2+b_0^2)\varphi_0^2+O(h). $$ Since we require that $\tilde{{\mathcal L}}$ be a perturbation of $L_-$, we must have $a_0^2+b_0^2=1$. This, together with \eqref{180} and \eqref{185} implies that $\sigma_0$ is completely determined by $\alpha_0$ and in fact, \begin{equation} \sigma_0^2+\alpha_0^2=\f{\dpr{1}{\varphi_0}^2}{\|\varphi_0\|^4}. \end{equation} We can rewrite the equation \eqref{151} equivalently as follows \begin{equation} (\tilde{{\mathcal L}}-i\alpha)[i (\varphi_{\alpha,1}+\varphi_{\alpha,2})+(\varphi_{\alpha,1}-\varphi_{\alpha,2})]=h(1+i) \end{equation} Denoting $q:=i(\varphi_{\alpha,1}+\varphi_{\alpha,2})+(\varphi_{\alpha,1}-\varphi_{\alpha,2})$, we see that we can write $\tilde{{\mathcal L}}=-\partial_x^2+1 - |q|^2$. In addition, $q$ has the representation \begin{equation} q=(c_0+c_1 h+O(h^2))\varphi_0+ h \Psi, \ \ \Psi\perp \varphi_0, \end{equation} where clearly $c_0=i(a_0+b_0)+(a_0-b_0)$ can be expressed in terms of $\alpha_0$. For example, $|c_0|^2=2(a_0^2+b_0^2)=2$. Compute \begin{eqnarray*} |q|^2 &=& |c_0|^2 \varphi_0^2 +2 h \varphi_0^2 \Re[c_0\bar{c_1}]+h\varphi_0[c_0\bar{\Psi}+\bar{c_0}\Psi]+O(h^2) \\ &=& 2 \varphi_0^2 + h V_\Psi+O(h^2), \end{eqnarray*} upon introducing $V_\Psi:=2 \varphi_0^2 \Re[c_0\bar{c_1}]+\varphi_0[c_0\bar{\Psi}+\bar{c_0}\Psi]$. It follows that $$ \tilde{{\mathcal L}}=-\partial_x^2+1 - |q|^2= L_- -h V_\Psi +O(h^2), $$ whence \eqref{190} becomes \begin{equation} (L_--h (V_\Psi+i \alpha_0) +O(h^2))((c_0+c_1 h+O(h^2))\varphi_0+ h \Psi)=h(1+i). \end{equation} In order to resolve this equation, we need to go in powers of $h$. The terms with power $h^0$ are clearly absent, due to $L_-[\varphi_0]=0$, which is just the profile equation. For the first order in $h$ terms, we have the equation \begin{equation} L_-\Psi-(V_\Psi+i \alpha_0)c_0 \varphi_0=1+i. \end{equation} Taking \eqref{220}, and its complex conjugate, and in addition the form of $V_\Psi$, $|c_0|^2=2$, we arrive at the system \begin{equation} \left(\begin{array}{cc} -\partial_x^2+1- 4\varphi_0^2 & -c_0^2 \varphi_0^2 \\ -\bar{c}_0^2 \varphi_0^2 & -\partial_x^2+1- 4\varphi_0^2 \end{array}\right) \left(\begin{array}{c} \Psi \\ \bar{\Psi} \end{array}\right)= \left(\begin{array}{c} 1+i +i \alpha_0 c_0 \varphi_0 +2 \varphi_0^3 c_0 \Re[c_0\bar{c_1}] \\ 1-i -i \alpha_0 \bar{c}_0 \varphi_0 + 2 \varphi_0^3 \bar{c}_0 \Re[c_0\bar{c_1}] \end{array}\right) \end{equation} Diagonalizing the system leads to the equations \begin{eqnarray} & & L_+[\bar{c}_0\Psi+c_0\bar{\Psi}]= c_0+\bar{c}_0+i(\bar{c}_0-c_0)+8 \varphi_0^3 \Re[c_0\bar{c_1}], \\ & & L_-[-\bar{c}_0\Psi+c_0\bar{\Psi}] = c_0-\bar{c}_0-i(c_0+\bar{c}_0)-4 i \alpha_0 \varphi_0. \end{eqnarray} Note that one solvability condition for \eqref{217} is exactly $\dpr{c_0-\bar{c}_0-i(c_0+\bar{c}_0)-4 i \alpha_0 \varphi_0}{\varphi_0}=0$. Elementary computations show that this is equivalent to $b_0 \dpr{1}{\varphi_0}=\alpha_0 \|\varphi_0\|^2$, which is exactly the relation \eqref{185}and \eqref{211}. The other relation, is that since $\Psi\perp \varphi_0$, we need to have $\bar{c}_0\Psi+c_0\bar{\Psi}\in \{\varphi_0\}^\perp$. This imposes the relation $L_+^{-1}[c_0+\bar{c}_0+i(\bar{c}_0-c_0)+8 \varphi_0^3 \Re[c_0\bar{c_1}]] \in \{\varphi_0\}^\perp$ or equivalently $$ [c_0+\bar{c}_0+i(\bar{c}_0-c_0)] \dpr{ L_+^{-1}[1]}{\varphi_0}+8 \Re[c_0\bar{c_1}]\dpr{L_+^{-1}[\varphi_0^3]}{\varphi_0}=0. $$ In fact, since $\dpr{ L_+^{-1}[1]}{\varphi_0}=0$ and $\dpr{L_+^{-1}[\varphi_0^3]}{\varphi_0}=-\f{1}{4} \dpr{\varphi_0}{\varphi_0}\neq 0$, it follows that $\Re[c_0\bar{c_1}]=0$. It even looks as if we have one degree of freedom, since $c_1$ is complex valued (and hence two parameters are involved). In the actual non-linear problem however, we need to involve a higher order solvability condition for \eqref{217}, which will finally yield the right number of relations.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1
nodes.statement: Let $\varphi_{\alpha}=\varphi_{\alpha, 1}+i\varphi_{\alpha, 2}$ be a solution of \eqref{110}. Then, we have \begin{equation} \left| \begin{array}{ll} \varphi_{\alpha,1}^{''}-\varphi_{\alpha,1}+2(\varphi_{\alpha,1}^2+\varphi_{\alpha, 2}^2)\varphi_{\alpha, 1}-\alpha\varphi_{\alpha, 2}=0 \\ \\ \varphi_{\alpha,2}^{''}-\varphi_{\alpha,2}+2(\varphi_{\alpha,1}^2+\varphi_{\alpha, 2}^2)\varphi_{\alpha, 2}+\alpha\varphi_{\alpha, 1}=0. \end{array} \right. \end{equation} Denoting the second order self-adjoint differential operator $L:=-\partial_x^2+1 - 2(\varphi_{\alpha,1}^2+\varphi_{\alpha, 2}^2)$, we see that \eqref{120} is a relationship in the form $$ \left| \begin{array}{l} L[\varphi_{\alpha,1}]=-\alpha \varphi_{\alpha,2} \\ L[\varphi_{\alpha,2}]=\alpha \varphi_{\alpha,1}. \end{array} \right. $$ Thus, applying $L$ to to first equation, we obtain $L^2[\varphi_{\alpha,1}]=-\alpha^2 \varphi_{\alpha,1}$. By taking a dot product with $\varphi_{\alpha,1}$, we obtain $$ 0\leq \|L \varphi_{\alpha,1}\|^2=\dpr{L^2[\varphi_{\alpha,1}]}{\varphi_{\alpha,1}}=-\alpha^2\|\varphi_{\alpha,1}\|^2<0, $$ which is a contradiction.

nodes.statement:
Note that $\varphi_0$ satisfies \eqref{1.1} with $h=0$, hence ${\mathcal L}_{-,0}[\varphi_0]=0$. Since $\varphi_0>0$, it follows by Sturm-Liouville theory that ${\mathcal L}_{-,0}\geq 0$ and $0$ is the bottom of the spectrum and ${\mathcal L}_{-,0}|_{\{\varphi_0\}^\perp}>0$. Next, we show the properties of ${\mathcal L}_{+,0}$. First, observe that the function $\varphi_0$ can be realized as a (rescaled) minimizer of the following constrained minimization problem  egin{equation} \left\{  egin{array}{l} \int_{-T}^T [(\varphi'(x))^2 - \varphi^4(x)] dx	o \min \ \int_{-T}^T \varphi^2(x) dx=1 \end{array} ight. \end{equation} Indeed, the existence of a minimizer of \eqref{30} is standard, moreover such minimizer is necessarily bell-shaped. Its Euler-Lagrange equation is in the form  egin{equation} \varphi''- 2 \varphi^3 = -\sigma \varphi, \end{equation} which has an unique (bell-shaped) solution, namely a rescaled version of $\varphi_0$. As a consequence of this, it is standard to show that $n({\mathcal L}_{+,0})=1$, since $\dpr{{\mathcal L}_{+,0} \varphi_0}{\varphi_0}<0$ and as a consequence of the minimization properties of $\varphi_0$, ${\mathcal L}_{+,0}|_{\{\varphi_0\}^\perp}\geq 0$. Also, by a direct differentiation of the profile equation \eqref{1.1} (with $h=0$), we conclude ${\mathcal L}_{+,0}[\varphi'_0]=0$. Finally, let us show that $Ker[{\mathcal L}_{+,0}]=span\{\varphi_0'\}$. In order to do that, we will show that the second independent solution of the equation ${\mathcal L}_{+,0}[g]=0$ does not belong to the space $L^2_{per.}[-T,T]$. Normally, such a solution $g$ can be written down by the reduction of order formula as follows $$ g(x)=\varphi'_0(x)\int_{a}^x  {1}{(\varphi'_0(y))^2} dy $$ The problem is that such a formula blows up whenever the interval of integration contains $0$. So, we use an alternative description of the eigenfunction, due to Rofe-Beketov, (see \cite{Teschl}, Exercise 5.11, p. 154) $$ g(x)=\varphi_0'(x) \int_0^x  {(2-6\varphi_0^2(y))((\varphi_0'(y))^2-(\varphi_0''(y))^2)}{((\varphi_0'(y))^2+(\varphi_0''(y))^2))^2} dy -  {\varphi_0''(x)}{(\varphi_0'(x))^2+(\varphi_0''(x))^2} $$ This function is well-defined and satisfies ${\mathcal L}_{+,0}[g]=0$. In order to show that the eigenvalue at zero is simple, it suffices to prove that $g$ is not $2T$ periodic. Clearly, the second part of the formula in $g$ is $2T$ periodic, so we concentrate on showing that the first piece, $g_1(x)$ is non-periodic. In fact, $g_1(-T)=g_1(T)$, since $\varphi_0'(T)=\varphi'_0(-T)=0$. We show that in fact $g_1'(-T)
eq g_1'(T)$. Since, $\varphi_0''(-T)=\varphi_0''(T)
eq 0$, it suffices to show that $$ \int_0^T  {(2-6\varphi_0^2(y))((\varphi_0'(y))^2-(\varphi_0''(y))^2)}{((\varphi_0'(y))^2+(\varphi_0''(y))^2))^2} dy
eq \int_0^{-T}  {(2-6\varphi_0^2(y))((\varphi_0'(y))^2-(\varphi_0''(y))^2)}{((\varphi_0'(y))^2+(\varphi_0''(y))^2))^2} dy. $$ Since the integrand is even, this is equivalent to  egin{equation} \int_0^T  {(2-6\varphi_0^2(y))((\varphi_0'(y))^2-(\varphi_0''(y))^2)}{((\varphi_0'(y))^2+(\varphi_0''(y))^2))^2} dy

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: By differentiating with respect to $h$ the profile equation, we obtain ${\mathcal L}_{+,h}[\partial_h \varphi_h]=1$. As a consequence, since we know $Ker[{\mathcal L}_{+,h}]=span[\varphi'_h]$ (and hence $1\perp Ker[{\mathcal L}_{+,h}]$), $$ \partial_h\varphi_h={\mathcal L}_{+,h}^{-1}[1]+\delta \varphi_h', $$ for some $\delta$. We claim $\delta=0$. Indeed, we know that $\varphi_h$ is an even function, and so is $\partial_h \varphi_h$. Clearly ${\mathcal L}_{+,h}$ (and its inverse on $Ker[{\mathcal L}_{+,h}]^\perp$) acts invariantly on the even subspace, so ${\mathcal L}_{+,h}^{-1}[1]$ is even as well. Thus, the odd piece $\delta \varphi_h'$ is actually zero, whence $\delta=0$. Thus, \begin{equation} \varphi_h=\varphi_0+h {\mathcal L}_{+,h}^{-1}[1]+O(h^2). \end{equation} Next, since ${\mathcal L}_{-,0}$ has a simple eigenvalue at zero, $L_{-,h}$ has a single eigenvalue close to zero, in the form $\lambda_0({\mathcal L}_{-,h})=a h+O(h^2)$. Say the corresponding eigenfunction is in the form $\varphi_0+ h z$, $z\in H^2[-T,T]$. Thus, \begin{equation} {\mathcal L}_{-,h}[\varphi_0+ h z]=a h(\varphi_0+ h z). \end{equation} However, by \eqref{35}, \begin{eqnarray*} {\mathcal L}_{-,h} &=&-\partial_x^2+1-2\varphi_h^2=-\partial_x^2+1-2 \varphi_0^2 - 4 h {\mathcal L}_{+,h}^{-1}[1] \varphi^0 +O(h^2)= \\ &=&{\mathcal L}_{-,0} - 4 h \varphi_0 {\mathcal L}_{+,h}^{-1}[1] +O(h^2). \end{eqnarray*} By taking the first order in $h$ terms in \eqref{40}, we obtain $$ {\mathcal L}_{-,0} z =4 \varphi_0^2 {\mathcal L}_{+,h}^{-1}[1] +a \varphi_0. $$ Now, take dot product with $\varphi_0$. Note that since $1\perp Ker[{\mathcal L}_{+,h}]$, we have that \\ ${\mathcal L}_{+,h}^{-1}[1]={\mathcal L}_{+,0}^{-1}[1]+O(h)$. Since $\dpr{{\mathcal L}_{-,0} z }{\varphi_0}= \dpr{ z }{{\mathcal L}_{-,0}[\varphi_0]}=0$, we obtain the relation $$ a\|\varphi_0\|^2+4 \dpr{\varphi_0^3}{{\mathcal L}_{+,0}^{-1}[1]}=0. $$ Thus, $ a=-\f{4}{\|\varphi_0\|^2} \dpr{{\mathcal L}_{+,0}^{-1}[\varphi_0^3]}{1}. $ However, the profile equation can be rewritten as $${\mathcal L}_{+,0}[\varphi_0]=-4 \varphi_0^3,$$ whence ${\mathcal L}_{+,0}^{-1}[\varphi_0^3]=-\f{1}{4} \varphi_0+\delta \varphi_0'$ and $$ a= \f{\int_{-T}^{T} \varphi_0(x)dx}{\int_{-T}^{T} \varphi_0^2 (x)dx}>0. $$ Also, $$ z={\mathcal L}_{-,0}^{-1}\left[4 \varphi_0^2 {\mathcal L}_{+,0}^{-1}[1] + \f{\int_{-T}^{T} \varphi_0(x)dx}{\int_{-T}^{T} \varphi_0^2 (x)dx} \varphi_0 \right]+O(h), $$ which is \eqref{28}.

nodes.statement: We now setup the full non-linear problem \eqref{151}, with $0<h<<1$, in the equivalent formulation \eqref{190}. More precisely, armed with the results from our informal analysis, we set the unknown function \\ $q=\varphi_{\alpha,1}-\varphi_{\alpha,2}+i(\varphi_{\alpha,1}+\varphi_{\alpha,2}) \in L^2_{per.}[-T,T]$ in the form $$ q=(c+d h)\varphi_0+ h \Psi, \Psi\perp \varphi_0 $$ where $$ c=a_0-b_0+i(a_0+b_0), $$ and $a_0, b_0$ are given by \eqref{180}, \eqref{185} and \eqref{211}), in terms of $\alpha_0$. Note that $|c|^2=2$. Also, in accordance with \eqref{211}, we require $\alpha_0: 0<\alpha_0 < \f{\dpr{1}{\varphi_0}}{\|\varphi_0\|^2}$. Now that we have set $q$ (and in particular $a_0, b_0$), we are looking for a scalar function $d=d(h)$ and a function $\Psi(h)\in \{\varphi_0\}^\perp$, so that \eqref{190} holds. We compute $$ |q|^2=2\varphi_0^2 +h V+h^2[|d|^2\varphi_0^2+\varphi_0(d \bar{\Psi}+\bar{d} \Psi) +|\Psi|^2], $$ where $$ V= 2 \varphi_0^2 \Re[c\bar{d}]+2 \varphi_0\Re[c \bar{\Psi}] $$ is a real-valued function as before. Introduce the {\it real-valued function} $$ G=G(d, \Psi)=|d|^2\varphi_0^2+\varphi_0(d \bar{\Psi}+\bar{d} \Psi) +|\Psi|^2. $$ We thus have a formula for $\tilde{{\mathcal L}}$ as follows $$ \tilde{{\mathcal L}}=-\partial_x^2+1- |q|^2= -\partial_x^2+1-2\varphi_0^2 - h V - h^2 G=L_- - h V -h^2 G. $$ Plugging this in \eqref{190}, we obtain the following relation \begin{equation} (L_- - h(V+i\alpha_0)-h^2 G)[(c+d h)\varphi_0+h \Psi]=h(1+i). \end{equation} After some algebraic manipulations, we obtain \begin{equation} L_- \Psi-c(V+i \alpha_0)\varphi_0-(1+i)-h[(V+i\alpha_0)(d \varphi_0 +\Psi)+c \varphi_0 G]=h^2 G(d, \Psi)\Psi. \end{equation} Similar to the derivation of \eqref{210}, we take \eqref{310} and its complex conjugate to obtain the following {\it non-linear} in $h$ system of equations \begin{eqnarray*} & & \left(\begin{array}{cc} -\partial_x^2+1- 4\varphi_0^2 & -c^2 \varphi_0^2 \\ -\bar{c}^2 \varphi_0^2 & -\partial_x^2+1- 4\varphi_0^2 \end{array}\right) \left(\begin{array}{c} \Psi \\ \bar{\Psi} \end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{c} 1+i +i \alpha_0 c \varphi_0 +2 \varphi_0^3 c \Re[c\bar{d}] \\ 1-i -i \alpha_0 \bar{c} \varphi_0 + 2 \varphi_0^3 \bar{c} \Re[c\bar{d}] \end{array}\right)+ \\ &+& h \left(\begin{array}{c} (V+i\alpha_0)(d\varphi_0 +\Psi)+c \varphi_0 G \\ (V-i\alpha_0)(\bar{d} \varphi_0 +\bar{\Psi})+\bar{c}\varphi_0 G \end{array}\right)+h^2 \left(\begin{array}{c} G(d, \Psi)\Psi \\G(d, \Psi)\bar{\Psi} \end{array}\right) \end{eqnarray*} Diagonalizing yields the equivalent equations \begin{eqnarray} L_+[\bar{c}\Psi+c\bar{\Psi}] &=& 4a_0 +8 \varphi_0^3 \Re[c\bar{d}]+h E_1(h,d,\Psi), \\ L_-[-\bar{c}\Psi+c\bar{\Psi}] &=& 4i( b_0- \alpha_0 \varphi_0) + \\ \nonumber &+& 2 i h[ V\varphi_0\Im[c\bar{d}]+V \Im[c\bar{\Psi}] - \alpha_0 \varphi_0\Re[c \bar{d}]-\alpha_0 \Re[c\bar{\Psi}]]+ h^2 E_2, \end{eqnarray} where $E_1,E_2$ are smooth functions of the respective arguments. This is the system that we need to solve - that is, the goal is to find a neighborhood $(0,h_0)$, so that for every $h\in (0,h_0)$, there is a scalar function $d=d(h)$ and a function $\Psi=\Psi(h)\in \{\varphi_0\}^\perp$, so that the pair satisfies the previous two relations. To that end, we shall use the implicit function theorem. It is clear that it is more convenient to introduce two real variables\footnote{recall that $c$ is already fixed in terms of $\alpha_0$, so finding $D_1, D_2$ is akin to finding the complex number $d$} $D_1:=\Re[c\bar{d}], D_2:=\Im[c\bar{d}]$. Clearly, the system requires some solvability conditions. We have already established that with our choice of $c$, we have that $c-\bar{c} -i(c+\bar{c})-4 i \alpha_0 \varphi_0\perp \varphi_0$. So, from \eqref{317}, we need to require \begin{eqnarray*} 0 &=& \dpr{V\varphi_0\Im(c\bar{d})+V \Im[c\bar{\Psi}]- \alpha_0 \varphi_0\Re[c \bar{d}]-\alpha_0 \Re [c\bar{\Psi}]}{\varphi_0}+O(h)= \\ &=& \dpr{D_2 V\varphi_0 - D_1 \alpha_0 \varphi_0 + V \Im[c\bar{\Psi}]}{\varphi_0}+O(h) \end{eqnarray*} In the last identity, we used that $\Psi\perp \varphi_0$, whence by the reality of $\varphi_0$, we have that $\bar{\Psi}\perp \varphi_0$ as well (and thus any linear combination of $\Psi, \bar{\Psi}$ is perpendicular to $\varphi_0$). Thus, we end up requiring \begin{equation} \dpr{D_2 V\varphi_0 - D_1 \alpha_0 \varphi_0 + V \Im[c\bar{\Psi}]}{\varphi_0}+O(h)=0 \end{equation} Since $\bar{c}\Psi+c\bar{\Psi}\perp \varphi_0$ , we need to have $$ 0=4 a_0 \dpr{L_+^{-1}[1]}{\varphi_0} +8 D_1 \dpr{L_+^{-1}[\varphi_0^3]}{1}+O(h). $$ Recalling that $\dpr{L_+^{-1}[1]}{\varphi_0}=0$ and $L_+[\varphi_0]=-4\varphi_0^3$, whence $L_+^{-1}[\varphi_0^3]=-\f{1}{4}\varphi_0$ and the previous relation reads \begin{equation} -2D_1 \dpr{\varphi_0}{1} +O(h)=0. \end{equation} The analysis so far allows us to solve the system\eqref{315}, \eqref{317}, for $h=0$. Namely, from \eqref{330}, we infer that \begin{equation} D_1^0=0 \end{equation} The next step is to find $\Psi^0$, from \eqref{315}and \eqref{317}, at $h=0$. Inverting $L_+$ in \eqref{315} and $L_-$ in \eqref{317} and taking the difference, and taking into account that $\Re[c\bar{d}]=D_1^0+O(h)=O(h)$, we obtain\footnote{Recall that $b_0-\alpha_0 \varphi_0\perp \varphi_0$, so taking $L_-^{-1}$ is justified. Similarly, with the definition of $D_1^0$ in \eqref{340}, taking $L_+^{-1}$ is justified as well.} \begin{equation} \Psi^0 = \f{4 a_0 L_+^{-1}[1]- 4 i L_-^{-1}[ b_0 - \alpha_0 \varphi_0]}{2\bar{c}}= c a_0 L_+^{-1}[1] - i c L_-^{-1}[ b_0 - \alpha_0\varphi_0]. \end{equation} Note that $\Psi^0\perp \varphi_0$ (as it should be), since $L_+^{-1}[1]\perp \varphi_0$, and $Image[ L_-^{-1}]\perp \varphi_0$. Finally, we use \eqref{320} to determine $D_2^0$. We obtain the formula \begin{equation} D_2^0\dpr{V^0 \varphi_0}{\varphi_0}=-\dpr{\Im[c\bar{\Psi}_0]}{V^0 \varphi_0}. \end{equation} We clearly need to compute $\Re[c\bar{\Psi}_0], \Im[c\bar{\Psi}_0]$. We have from \eqref{350}, \begin{eqnarray*} \Re[c\bar{\Psi}_0] &=& 2 a_0 L_+^{-1}[1], \\ \Im[c\bar{\Psi}_0]&=& 2 L_-^{-1}[b_0-\alpha_0 \varphi_0]. \end{eqnarray*} According to its definition $$ V^0=V(0, \Psi_0)=2 \varphi_0^2 D_1^0+\varphi_0[c \bar{\Psi^0}+\bar{c}\Psi^0]=2\varphi_0\Re[c\bar{\Psi}_0]= 2 a_0 \varphi_0 L_+^{-1}[1]. $$ Consequently, since $L_+^{-1}[\varphi_0^3]=-\f{1}{4} \varphi_0$, \begin{equation} \dpr{V^0 \varphi_0}{\varphi_0} = 4 a_0 \dpr{\varphi_0^3}{L_+^{-1}[1]}= - a_0 \dpr{1}{\varphi_0}. \end{equation} Finally, \begin{eqnarray*} \dpr{\Im[c\bar{\Psi}_0]}{V^0 \varphi_0} = 8 a_0 \dpr{\varphi_0^2 L_+^{-1}[1]}{L_-^{-1}[b_0-\alpha_0 \varphi_0]}. \end{eqnarray*} From \eqref{c:14}, we deduce \begin{equation} D_2^0= 8 \f{\dpr{\varphi_0^2 L_+^{-1}[1]}{L_-^{-1}[b_0-\alpha_0 \varphi_0]}}{\dpr{1}{\varphi_0}} \end{equation} To recapitulate, we have determined, in \eqref{350}, together with $D_1^0, D_2^0$ as determined above, the unique solutions of \eqref{315} and \eqref{317}, when $h=0$. We now setup the implicit function argument, which will work in a neighborhood of the solution $h=0$, $\Psi^0$, given by \eqref{350}, and $ D_1^0, D_2^0$. First, we set the solvability condition arising in \eqref{317}, namely the scalar function\footnote{Here we use again that $\dpr{ \Im[c\bar{\Psi}]}{\varphi_0}=0$} \begin{eqnarray*} & & Q_1(h; \Psi, D_1, D_2) = 2i\dpr{D_2 V(D_1, \Psi)\varphi_0 +V \Im[c\bar{\Psi}] - \alpha_0 \varphi_0 D_1 -\alpha_0 \Im[c\bar{\Psi}]}{\varphi_0}+ \\ &+& h \dpr{E_2(h,\Psi, D_1, D_2)}{\varphi_0} = 2i\dpr{D_2 V(D_1, \Psi)\varphi_0 + V(D_1, \Psi) \Im[c\bar{\Psi}] - \alpha_0 \varphi_0D_1 }{\varphi_0}+\\ &+& h \dpr{E_2(h,\Psi, D_1, D_2)}{\varphi_0}, \end{eqnarray*} where $V(D_1, \Psi)=2 D_1 \varphi_0^2 + \varphi_0(\bar{c} \Psi+c \bar{\Psi})$. The other function is constructed as follows - apply $L_+^{-1}$ in \eqref{315} and $L_-^{-1}$ in \eqref{317} (once we make sure that the right hand side is orthogonal to $\varphi_0$). After subtracting and simplifying, \begin{eqnarray*} & & Q_2(h; \Psi, D_1, D_2) = 2 \bar{c} \Psi -\left[ 4 a_0 L_+^{-1}[1] - 2 D_1 \varphi_0 +h L_+^{-1}[E_1(h; \Psi, D_1,D_2)] \right] +4i L_-^{-1}[b_0 - \alpha_0 \varphi_0] \\ & & + L_-^{-1}[P_{\{\varphi_0\}^\perp}[2 i h(D_2 V(D_1, \Psi) \varphi_0 -D_1 \alpha_0\varphi_0+V(D_1, \Psi) \Im[c\bar{\Psi}]-\alpha_0 \Im[c\bar{\Psi}])+h^2 E_2(h; \Psi, D_1,D_2) ]]. \end{eqnarray*} Note that the projection $P_{\{\varphi_0\}^\perp}$ becomes irrelevant, once we impose the condition \\ $Q_1(h; \Psi, D_1, D_2)=0$! On the other hand, we need it in the definition of $Q_2$ to keep it well-defined, even when $Q_1(h; \Psi, D_1, D_2)=0$ is not enforced. We now consider $$ (Q_1, Q_2)(h; \Psi, D_1, D_2): \mathbf R\times \{\varphi_0\}^\perp \times \mathbf R\times \mathbf R \to \mathbf R\times L^2_{per.}[-T,T] $$ and we would like to solve \begin{equation} \left| \begin{array}{c} Q_1(h; \Psi, D_1, D_2)=0 \\ Q_2(h; \Psi, D_1, D_2)=0. \end{array} \right. \end{equation} Note that if one obtains solutions to \eqref{485}, the projection $P_{\{\varphi_0\}^\perp}$ becomes irrelevant and the system $Q_1=Q_2=0$ becomes equivalent to the system \eqref{315}and \eqref{317}. Observe that by our earlier considerations, for $h=0$, we have a solution, that is $$ \left| \begin{array}{c} Q_1(0; \Psi^0, 0, D_2^0)=0 \\ Q_2(0; \Psi^0, 0, D_2^0)=0, \end{array} \right. $$ where $Q_2^0$ is given in \eqref{c:17}. Our construction of the family $\Psi(h), D_1(h), D_2(h)$ in a neighborhood $(0,h_0)$ will follow, once we can verify that $$ d(Q_1, Q_2)(0; \Psi^0, 0, D_2^0)[\cdot, \cdot, \cdot]: \{\varphi_0\}^\perp \times \mathbf R\times \mathbf R \to \mathbf R\times L^2_{per.}[-T,T] $$ is an isomorphism. That is, for every $\chi\in L^2_{per.}[-T,T]$ and $z\in \mathbf R$, there must be unique solution $\psi\in \{\varphi_0\}^\perp, d_1 \in \mathbf R, d_2\in \mathbf R$ of the linear system \begin{eqnarray*} & & dQ_1(0; \Psi^0, 0, D_2^0)[\psi, d_1, d_2]=z \\ & & dQ_2(0; \Psi^0, 0, D_2^0)[\psi, d_1, d_2]=\chi \end{eqnarray*} so that the linear mapping $(\chi, z)\to (\psi(\chi, z), d_1(\chi, z), d_2(\chi, z))$ is continuous. First, we compute $dQ_2(0; \Psi^0, 0, D_2^0)[\psi, d_1, d_2]= 2\bar{c} \psi + 2 d_1 \varphi_0$. In order to prepare the calculation for $ dQ_1(0; \Psi^0,0, D_2^0)[\psi, d_1, d_2]$, observe that \begin{eqnarray*} V(D_1, \Psi) &=& 2 D_1 \varphi_0^2+2\varphi_0 \Re[c\bar{\Psi}] \\ dV(0,\Psi^0)(d_1, \psi) &=& 2 d_1 \varphi_0^2+2\varphi_0 \Re[c\bar{\psi}] \end{eqnarray*} Consequently, \begin{eqnarray*} & & dQ_1(0; \Psi^0,0, D_2^0)[\psi, d_1, d_2] = 2i\dpr{d_2 V^0\varphi_0+ D_2^0(2 d_1\varphi_0^2+2\varphi_0\Re[c\bar{\psi}])}{\varphi_0}+ \\ &+& 2i\dpr{(2 d_1 \varphi_0^2+2\varphi_0\Re[c\bar{\psi}]) \Im[c\bar{\Psi}_0]}{\varphi_0} +2i \dpr{V^0 \Im[c\bar{\psi}]}{\varphi_0} - 2i \alpha_0 d_1 \|\varphi_0\|^2. \end{eqnarray*} Now, the equation $\chi=dQ_2(0; \Psi^0, 0, D_2^0)[\psi, d_1, d_2]$, has the form \begin{eqnarray*} & &\chi= dQ_2(0; \Psi^0, 0, D_2^0)[\psi, d_1, d_2]= 2\bar{c} \psi + 2 d_1 \varphi_0. \end{eqnarray*} It clearly has the unique solution $$ d_1=\f{\dpr{\chi}{\varphi_0}}{2\|\varphi_0\|^2}, \psi=\f{1}{2\bar{c}}(\chi- 2d_1 \varphi_0)\in \{\varphi_0\}^\perp $$ Plugging the expressions for $d_1$ and $\psi$ in the equation $dQ_1=z$ produces a linear equation for $d_2$, once we take a dot product with $\varphi_0$. More precisely, \begin{eqnarray*} d_2 \dpr{V^0\varphi_0}{\varphi_0} &=& \f{z}{2i} -\dpr{D_2^0(2 d_1\varphi_0^2+2\varphi_0\Re[c\bar{\psi}])}{\varphi_0} - \dpr{(2 d_1 \varphi_0^2+2\varphi_0\Re[c\bar{\psi}]) \Im[c\bar{\Psi}_0]}{\varphi_0} +\\ &+& \alpha_0 d_1 \|\varphi_0\|^2 - \dpr{V^0 \Im[c\bar{\psi}]}{\varphi_0} \end{eqnarray*} which has also unique solution, provided the coefficient in front of it, $\dpr{V^0 \varphi_0}{\varphi_0}\neq 0$ is non-zero. But we have already verfied that, see \eqref{c:27}. We also see that the solution $d_2$ depends linearly, through a nice formula on $\chi, z$. It follows that the mapping $(\chi, z)\to (\psi, d_1, d_2)$ is indeed an isomorphism, in the sense specified above. The implicit function theorem thus applies and we have constructed the solutions. It remains to verify the formulas \eqref{500}and \eqref{510}. First, we have that $c\bar{d}=D_1^0+i D_2^0+O(h)=i D_2^0+O(h)$, whence \begin{equation} d^0= - \f{i c}{2} D_2^0=\f{a_0+b_0}{2} D_2^0 +i\f{b_0-a_0}{2} D_2^0. \end{equation} Thus, starting with the relation $\varphi_{\alpha,1}-\varphi_{\alpha,2}+i (\varphi_{\alpha,1}-\varphi_{\alpha,2})=q=(c+d h)\varphi_0 +h \Psi$, we deduce \begin{eqnarray*} \varphi_{\alpha,1} &=& (a_0+\f{b_0}{2} h D_2^0)\varphi_0 +h(a_0^2 L_+^{-1}[1]+b_0 L_-^{-1}[b_0-\alpha_0 \varphi_0]) +O(h^2)\\ \varphi_{\alpha,2} &=&(b_0-\f{a_0}{2} h D_2^0)\varphi_0 +h(a_0 b_0 L_+^{-1}[1]-a_0 L_-^{-1}[b_0-\alpha_0 \varphi_0]) +O(h^2), \end{eqnarray*} which is the final claim in Theorem \ref{102}.
nodes.section: 3.2 Solutions of 3.2 - rigorous construction
nodes.statement_short: Implicit function theorem around h=0 for the unknowns (Psi, D_1, D_2). The key step is that the linearization at (Psi^0,0,D_2^0) is an isomorphism because <V^0 phi_0,phi_0> = -a_0<1,phi_0> is nonzero.

nodes.name: Ansatz for q
nodes.statement: We now setup the full non-linear problem \eqref{151}, with $0<h<<1$, in the equivalent formulation \eqref{190}. More precisely, armed with the results from our informal analysis, we set the unknown function \\ $q=\varphi_{\alpha,1}-\varphi_{\alpha,2}+i(\varphi_{\alpha,1}+\varphi_{\alpha,2}) \in L^2_{per.}[-T,T]$ in the form $$ q=(c+d h)\varphi_0+ h \Psi, \Psi\perp \varphi_0 $$ where $$ c=a_0-b_0+i(a_0+b_0), $$ and $a_0, b_0$ are given by \eqref{180}, \eqref{185} and \eqref{211}), in terms of $\alpha_0$. Note that $|c|^2=2$. Also, in accordance with \eqref{211}, we require $\alpha_0: 0<\alpha_0 < \f{\dpr{1}{\varphi_0}}{\|\varphi_0\|^2}$.

nodes.statement_short: Set q=(c+dh)phi_0+h Psi with c fixed by alpha_0, |c|^2=2.

nodes.name: Unknowns
nodes.statement: Now that we have set $q$ (and in particular $a_0, b_0$), we are looking for a scalar function $d=d(h)$ and a function $\Psi(h)\in \{\varphi_0\}^\perp$, so that \eqref{190} holds.

nodes.statement_short: Seek d(h) and Psi(h) orthogonal to phi_0.

nodes.name: Expand |q|^2 and tilde L
nodes.statement: We compute $$ |q|^2=2\varphi_0^2 +h V+h^2[|d|^2\varphi_0^2+\varphi_0(d \bar{\Psi}+\bar{d} \Psi) +|\Psi|^2], $$ where $$ V= 2 \varphi_0^2 \Re[c\bar{d}]+2 \varphi_0\Re[c \bar{\Psi}] $$ is a real-valued function as before. Introduce the {\it real-valued function} $$ G=G(d, \Psi)=|d|^2\varphi_0^2+\varphi_0(d \bar{\Psi}+\bar{d} \Psi) +|\Psi|^2. $$ We thus have a formula for $\tilde{{\mathcal L}}$ as follows $$ \tilde{{\mathcal L}}=-\partial_x^2+1- |q|^2= -\partial_x^2+1-2\varphi_0^2 - h V - h^2 G=L_- - h V -h^2 G. $$

nodes.statement_short: Expand |q|^2 and tilde L in h with V and G.

nodes.name: Equation for Psi
nodes.statement: Plugging this in \eqref{190}, we obtain the following relation \begin{equation} (L_- - h(V+i\alpha_0)-h^2 G)[(c+d h)\varphi_0+h \Psi]=h(1+i). \end{equation} After some algebraic manipulations, we obtain \begin{equation} L_- \Psi-c(V+i \alpha_0)\varphi_0-(1+i)-h[(V+i\alpha_0)(d \varphi_0 +\Psi)+c \varphi_0 G]=h^2 G(d, \Psi)\Psi. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3.2 Solutions of 3.2 - rigorous construction
nodes.statement_short: Substitute into (3.12) and divide by h.

nodes.name: Diagonalize
nodes.statement: Similar to the derivation of \eqref{210}, we take \eqref{310} and its complex conjugate to obtain the following {\it non-linear} in $h$ system of equations \begin{eqnarray*} & & \left(\begin{array}{cc} -\partial_x^2+1- 4\varphi_0^2 & -c^2 \varphi_0^2 \\ -\bar{c}^2 \varphi_0^2 & -\partial_x^2+1- 4\varphi_0^2 \end{array}\right) \left(\begin{array}{c} \Psi \\ \bar{\Psi} \end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{c} 1+i +i \alpha_0 c \varphi_0 +2 \varphi_0^3 c \Re[c\bar{d}] \\ 1-i -i \alpha_0 \bar{c} \varphi_0 + 2 \varphi_0^3 \bar{c} \Re[c\bar{d}] \end{array}\right)+ \\ &+& h \left(\begin{array}{c} (V+i\alpha_0)(d\varphi_0 +\Psi)+c \varphi_0 G \\ (V-i\alpha_0)(\bar{d} \varphi_0 +\bar{\Psi})+\bar{c}\varphi_0 G \end{array}\right)+h^2 \left(\begin{array}{c} G(d, \Psi)\Psi \\G(d, \Psi)\bar{\Psi} \end{array}\right) \end{eqnarray*} Diagonalizing yields the equivalent equations \begin{eqnarray} L_+[\bar{c}\Psi+c\bar{\Psi}] &=& 4a_0 +8 \varphi_0^3 \Re[c\bar{d}]+h E_1(h,d,\Psi), \\ L_-[-\bar{c}\Psi+c\bar{\Psi}] &=& 4i( b_0- \alpha_0 \varphi_0) + \\ \nonumber &+& 2 i h[ V\varphi_0\Im[c\bar{d}]+V \Im[c\bar{\Psi}] - \alpha_0 \varphi_0\Re[c \bar{d}]-\alpha_0 \Re[c\bar{\Psi}]]+ h^2 E_2, \end{eqnarray} where $E_1,E_2$ are smooth functions of the respective arguments.

nodes.statement_short: Take complex conjugate and diagonalize into L_+ and L_- equations.

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: This is the system that we need to solve - that is, the goal is to find a neighborhood $(0,h_0)$, so that for every $h\in (0,h_0)$, there is a scalar function $d=d(h)$ and a function $\Psi=\Psi(h)\in \{\varphi_0\}^\perp$, so that the pair satisfies the previous two relations.

nodes.statement_short: Find d(h), Psi(h) for h in (0,h_0).

nodes.name: Real unknowns D_1, D_2
nodes.statement: To that end, we shall use the implicit function theorem. It is clear that it is more convenient to introduce two real variables\footnote{recall that $c$ is already fixed in terms of $\alpha_0$, so finding $D_1, D_2$ is akin to finding the complex number $d$} $D_1:=\Re[c\bar{d}], D_2:=\Im[c\bar{d}]$.
nodes.section: 3.2 Solutions of 3.2 - rigorous construction
nodes.statement_short: Plan the implicit function theorem and introduce D_1, D_2.

nodes.name: Solvability from L_- equation
nodes.statement: Clearly, the system requires some solvability conditions. We have already established that with our choice of $c$, we have that $c-\bar{c} -i(c+\bar{c})-4 i \alpha_0 \varphi_0\perp \varphi_0$. So, from \eqref{317}, we need to require \begin{eqnarray*} 0 &=& \dpr{V\varphi_0\Im(c\bar{d})+V \Im[c\bar{\Psi}]- \alpha_0 \varphi_0\Re[c \bar{d}]-\alpha_0 \Re [c\bar{\Psi}]}{\varphi_0}+O(h)= \\ &=& \dpr{D_2 V\varphi_0 - D_1 \alpha_0 \varphi_0 + V \Im[c\bar{\Psi}]}{\varphi_0}+O(h) \end{eqnarray*} In the last identity, we used that $\Psi\perp \varphi_0$, whence by the reality of $\varphi_0$, we have that $\bar{\Psi}\perp \varphi_0$ as well (and thus any linear combination of $\Psi, \bar{\Psi}$ is perpendicular to $\varphi_0$). Thus, we end up requiring \begin{equation} \dpr{D_2 V\varphi_0 - D_1 \alpha_0 \varphi_0 + V \Im[c\bar{\Psi}]}{\varphi_0}+O(h)=0 \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3.2 Solutions of 3.2 - rigorous construction
nodes.statement_short: Orthogonality to phi_0 in (3.22) yields (3.23).

nodes.name: Solvability from L_+ equation
nodes.statement: Since $\bar{c}\Psi+c\bar{\Psi}\perp \varphi_0$ , we need to have $$ 0=4 a_0 \dpr{L_+^{-1}[1]}{\varphi_0} +8 D_1 \dpr{L_+^{-1}[\varphi_0^3]}{1}+O(h). $$ Recalling that $\dpr{L_+^{-1}[1]}{\varphi_0}=0$ and $L_+[\varphi_0]=-4\varphi_0^3$, whence $L_+^{-1}[\varphi_0^3]=-\f{1}{4}\varphi_0$ and the previous relation reads \begin{equation} -2D_1 \dpr{\varphi_0}{1} +O(h)=0. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3.2 Solutions of 3.2 - rigorous construction
nodes.statement_short: Orthogonality in (3.21) yields -2D_1<phi_0,1>+O(h)=0.

nodes.name: D_1^0=0
nodes.statement: The analysis so far allows us to solve the system\eqref{315}, \eqref{317}, for $h=0$. Namely, from \eqref{330}, we infer that \begin{equation} D_1^0=0 \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3.2 Solutions of 3.2 - rigorous construction

nodes.name: Compute Psi^0
nodes.statement: The next step is to find $\Psi^0$, from \eqref{315}and \eqref{317}, at $h=0$. Inverting $L_+$ in \eqref{315} and $L_-$ in \eqref{317} and taking the difference, and taking into account that $\Re[c\bar{d}]=D_1^0+O(h)=O(h)$, we obtain\footnote{Recall that $b_0-\alpha_0 \varphi_0\perp \varphi_0$, so taking $L_-^{-1}$ is justified. Similarly, with the definition of $D_1^0$ in \eqref{340}, taking $L_+^{-1}$ is justified as well.} \begin{equation} \Psi^0 = \f{4 a_0 L_+^{-1}[1]- 4 i L_-^{-1}[ b_0 - \alpha_0 \varphi_0]}{2\bar{c}}= c a_0 L_+^{-1}[1] - i c L_-^{-1}[ b_0 - \alpha_0\varphi_0]. \end{equation} Note that $\Psi^0\perp \varphi_0$ (as it should be), since $L_+^{-1}[1]\perp \varphi_0$, and $Image[ L_-^{-1}]\perp \varphi_0$.
nodes.section: 3.2 Solutions of 3.2 - rigorous construction
nodes.statement_short: Invert L_+ and L_- at h=0 to get Psi^0.

nodes.name: Equation for D_2^0
nodes.statement: Finally, we use \eqref{320} to determine $D_2^0$. We obtain the formula \begin{equation} D_2^0\dpr{V^0 \varphi_0}{\varphi_0}=-\dpr{\Im[c\bar{\Psi}_0]}{V^0 \varphi_0}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3.2 Solutions of 3.2 - rigorous construction
nodes.statement_short: Solvability (3.23) at h=0 gives (3.27).

nodes.name: Compute D_2^0
nodes.statement: We clearly need to compute $\Re[c\bar{\Psi}_0], \Im[c\bar{\Psi}_0]$. We have from \eqref{350}, \begin{eqnarray*} \Re[c\bar{\Psi}_0] &=& 2 a_0 L_+^{-1}[1], \\ \Im[c\bar{\Psi}_0]&=& 2 L_-^{-1}[b_0-\alpha_0 \varphi_0]. \end{eqnarray*} According to its definition $$ V^0=V(0, \Psi_0)=2 \varphi_0^2 D_1^0+\varphi_0[c \bar{\Psi^0}+\bar{c}\Psi^0]=2\varphi_0\Re[c\bar{\Psi}_0]= 2 a_0 \varphi_0 L_+^{-1}[1]. $$ Consequently, since $L_+^{-1}[\varphi_0^3]=-\f{1}{4} \varphi_0$, \begin{equation} \dpr{V^0 \varphi_0}{\varphi_0} = 4 a_0 \dpr{\varphi_0^3}{L_+^{-1}[1]}= - a_0 \dpr{1}{\varphi_0}. \end{equation} Finally, \begin{eqnarray*} \dpr{\Im[c\bar{\Psi}_0]}{V^0 \varphi_0} = 8 a_0 \dpr{\varphi_0^2 L_+^{-1}[1]}{L_-^{-1}[b_0-\alpha_0 \varphi_0]}. \end{eqnarray*} From \eqref{c:14}, we deduce \begin{equation} D_2^0= 8 \f{\dpr{\varphi_0^2 L_+^{-1}[1]}{L_-^{-1}[b_0-\alpha_0 \varphi_0]}}{\dpr{1}{\varphi_0}} \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3.2 Solutions of 3.2 - rigorous construction
nodes.statement_short: Evaluate the inner products to get D_2^0 in closed form.

nodes.name: Unique solution at h=0
nodes.statement: To recapitulate, we have determined, in \eqref{350}, together with $D_1^0, D_2^0$ as determined above, the unique solutions of \eqref{315} and \eqref{317}, when $h=0$. We now setup the implicit function argument, which will work in a neighborhood of the solution $h=0$, $\Psi^0$, given by \eqref{350}, and $ D_1^0, D_2^0$.
nodes.section: 3.2 Solutions of 3.2 - rigorous construction
nodes.statement_short: At h=0 the system has the solution (Psi^0, 0, D_2^0).

nodes.name: Define Q_1
nodes.statement: First, we set the solvability condition arising in \eqref{317}, namely the scalar function\footnote{Here we use again that $\dpr{ \Im[c\bar{\Psi}]}{\varphi_0}=0$} \begin{eqnarray*} & & Q_1(h; \Psi, D_1, D_2) = 2i\dpr{D_2 V(D_1, \Psi)\varphi_0 +V \Im[c\bar{\Psi}] - \alpha_0 \varphi_0 D_1 -\alpha_0 \Im[c\bar{\Psi}]}{\varphi_0}+ \\ &+& h \dpr{E_2(h,\Psi, D_1, D_2)}{\varphi_0} = 2i\dpr{D_2 V(D_1, \Psi)\varphi_0 + V(D_1, \Psi) \Im[c\bar{\Psi}] - \alpha_0 \varphi_0D_1 }{\varphi_0}+\\ &+& h \dpr{E_2(h,\Psi, D_1, D_2)}{\varphi_0}, \end{eqnarray*} where $V(D_1, \Psi)=2 D_1 \varphi_0^2 + \varphi_0(\bar{c} \Psi+c \bar{\Psi})$.
nodes.section: 3.2 Solutions of 3.2 - rigorous construction
nodes.statement_short: Scalar solvability function Q_1.

nodes.name: Define Q_2
nodes.statement: The other function is constructed as follows - apply $L_+^{-1}$ in \eqref{315} and $L_-^{-1}$ in \eqref{317} (once we make sure that the right hand side is orthogonal to $\varphi_0$). After subtracting and simplifying, \begin{eqnarray*} & & Q_2(h; \Psi, D_1, D_2) = 2 \bar{c} \Psi -\left[ 4 a_0 L_+^{-1}[1] - 2 D_1 \varphi_0 +h L_+^{-1}[E_1(h; \Psi, D_1,D_2)] \right] +4i L_-^{-1}[b_0 - \alpha_0 \varphi_0] \\ & & + L_-^{-1}[P_{\{\varphi_0\}^\perp}[2 i h(D_2 V(D_1, \Psi) \varphi_0 -D_1 \alpha_0\varphi_0+V(D_1, \Psi) \Im[c\bar{\Psi}]-\alpha_0 \Im[c\bar{\Psi}])+h^2 E_2(h; \Psi, D_1,D_2) ]]. \end{eqnarray*} Note that the projection $P_{\{\varphi_0\}^\perp}$ becomes irrelevant, once we impose the condition \\ $Q_1(h; \Psi, D_1, D_2)=0$! On the other hand, we need it in the definition of $Q_2$ to keep it well-defined, even when $Q_1(h; \Psi, D_1, D_2)=0$ is not enforced.
nodes.section: 3.2 Solutions of 3.2 - rigorous construction
nodes.statement_short: Function Q_2 from inverting L_+ and L_- with projection.

nodes.name: Reformulated system
nodes.statement: We now consider $$ (Q_1, Q_2)(h; \Psi, D_1, D_2): \mathbf R\times \{\varphi_0\}^\perp \times \mathbf R\times \mathbf R \to \mathbf R\times L^2_{per.}[-T,T] $$ and we would like to solve \begin{equation} \left| \begin{array}{c} Q_1(h; \Psi, D_1, D_2)=0 \\ Q_2(h; \Psi, D_1, D_2)=0. \end{array} \right. \end{equation} Note that if one obtains solutions to \eqref{485}, the projection $P_{\{\varphi_0\}^\perp}$ becomes irrelevant and the system $Q_1=Q_2=0$ becomes equivalent to the system \eqref{315}and \eqref{317}.
nodes.section: 3.2 Solutions of 3.2 - rigorous construction
nodes.statement_short: Solve Q_1=Q_2=0, equivalent to (3.21)-(3.22).

nodes.name: Base point
nodes.statement: Observe that by our earlier considerations, for $h=0$, we have a solution, that is $$ \left| \begin{array}{c} Q_1(0; \Psi^0, 0, D_2^0)=0 \\ Q_2(0; \Psi^0, 0, D_2^0)=0, \end{array} \right. $$ where $Q_2^0$ is given in \eqref{c:17}.
nodes.section: 3.2 Solutions of 3.2 - rigorous construction
nodes.statement_short: The h=0 solution solves Q_1=Q_2=0.

nodes.name: Reduce to invertibility of the differential
nodes.statement: Our construction of the family $\Psi(h), D_1(h), D_2(h)$ in a neighborhood $(0,h_0)$ will follow, once we can verify that $$ d(Q_1, Q_2)(0; \Psi^0, 0, D_2^0)[\cdot, \cdot, \cdot]: \{\varphi_0\}^\perp \times \mathbf R\times \mathbf R \to \mathbf R\times L^2_{per.}[-T,T] $$ is an isomorphism. That is, for every $\chi\in L^2_{per.}[-T,T]$ and $z\in \mathbf R$, there must be unique solution $\psi\in \{\varphi_0\}^\perp, d_1 \in \mathbf R, d_2\in \mathbf R$ of the linear system \begin{eqnarray*} & & dQ_1(0; \Psi^0, 0, D_2^0)[\psi, d_1, d_2]=z \\ & & dQ_2(0; \Psi^0, 0, D_2^0)[\psi, d_1, d_2]=\chi \end{eqnarray*} so that the linear mapping $(\chi, z)\to (\psi(\chi, z), d_1(\chi, z), d_2(\chi, z))$ is continuous.
nodes.section: 3.2 Solutions of 3.2 - rigorous construction
nodes.statement_short: It suffices that d(Q_1,Q_2) at the base point is an isomorphism.

nodes.name: Compute the differential
nodes.statement: First, we compute $dQ_2(0; \Psi^0, 0, D_2^0)[\psi, d_1, d_2]= 2\bar{c} \psi + 2 d_1 \varphi_0$. In order to prepare the calculation for $ dQ_1(0; \Psi^0,0, D_2^0)[\psi, d_1, d_2]$, observe that \begin{eqnarray*} V(D_1, \Psi) &=& 2 D_1 \varphi_0^2+2\varphi_0 \Re[c\bar{\Psi}] \\ dV(0,\Psi^0)(d_1, \psi) &=& 2 d_1 \varphi_0^2+2\varphi_0 \Re[c\bar{\psi}] \end{eqnarray*} Consequently, \begin{eqnarray*} & & dQ_1(0; \Psi^0,0, D_2^0)[\psi, d_1, d_2] = 2i\dpr{d_2 V^0\varphi_0+ D_2^0(2 d_1\varphi_0^2+2\varphi_0\Re[c\bar{\psi}])}{\varphi_0}+ \\ &+& 2i\dpr{(2 d_1 \varphi_0^2+2\varphi_0\Re[c\bar{\psi}]) \Im[c\bar{\Psi}_0]}{\varphi_0} +2i \dpr{V^0 \Im[c\bar{\psi}]}{\varphi_0} - 2i \alpha_0 d_1 \|\varphi_0\|^2. \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.section: 3.2 Solutions of 3.2 - rigorous construction
nodes.statement_short: Compute dQ_2 and dQ_1.

nodes.name: Solve for d_1, psi
nodes.statement: Now, the equation $\chi=dQ_2(0; \Psi^0, 0, D_2^0)[\psi, d_1, d_2]$, has the form \begin{eqnarray*} & &\chi= dQ_2(0; \Psi^0, 0, D_2^0)[\psi, d_1, d_2]= 2\bar{c} \psi + 2 d_1 \varphi_0. \end{eqnarray*} It clearly has the unique solution $$ d_1=\f{\dpr{\chi}{\varphi_0}}{2\|\varphi_0\|^2}, \psi=\f{1}{2\bar{c}}(\chi- 2d_1 \varphi_0)\in \{\varphi_0\}^\perp $$
nodes.section: 3.2 Solutions of 3.2 - rigorous construction
nodes.statement_short: dQ_2 = chi has a unique explicit solution.

nodes.name: Isomorphism and IFT
nodes.statement: Plugging the expressions for $d_1$ and $\psi$ in the equation $dQ_1=z$ produces a linear equation for $d_2$, once we take a dot product with $\varphi_0$. More precisely, \begin{eqnarray*} d_2 \dpr{V^0\varphi_0}{\varphi_0} &=& \f{z}{2i} -\dpr{D_2^0(2 d_1\varphi_0^2+2\varphi_0\Re[c\bar{\psi}])}{\varphi_0} - \dpr{(2 d_1 \varphi_0^2+2\varphi_0\Re[c\bar{\psi}]) \Im[c\bar{\Psi}_0]}{\varphi_0} +\\ &+& \alpha_0 d_1 \|\varphi_0\|^2 - \dpr{V^0 \Im[c\bar{\psi}]}{\varphi_0} \end{eqnarray*} which has also unique solution, provided the coefficient in front of it, $\dpr{V^0 \varphi_0}{\varphi_0}\neq 0$ is non-zero. But we have already verfied that, see \eqref{c:27}. We also see that the solution $d_2$ depends linearly, through a nice formula on $\chi, z$. It follows that the mapping $(\chi, z)\to (\psi, d_1, d_2)$ is indeed an isomorphism, in the sense specified above. The implicit function theorem thus applies and we have constructed the solutions.
nodes.section: 3.2 Solutions of 3.2 - rigorous construction
nodes.statement_short: d_2 is determined since <V^0phi_0,phi_0> != 0; the implicit function theorem applies.

nodes.name: Taylor expansions
nodes.statement: It remains to verify the formulas \eqref{500}and \eqref{510}. First, we have that $c\bar{d}=D_1^0+i D_2^0+O(h)=i D_2^0+O(h)$, whence \begin{equation} d^0= - \f{i c}{2} D_2^0=\f{a_0+b_0}{2} D_2^0 +i\f{b_0-a_0}{2} D_2^0. \end{equation} Thus, starting with the relation $\varphi_{\alpha,1}-\varphi_{\alpha,2}+i (\varphi_{\alpha,1}-\varphi_{\alpha,2})=q=(c+d h)\varphi_0 +h \Psi$, we deduce \begin{eqnarray*} \varphi_{\alpha,1} &=& (a_0+\f{b_0}{2} h D_2^0)\varphi_0 +h(a_0^2 L_+^{-1}[1]+b_0 L_-^{-1}[b_0-\alpha_0 \varphi_0]) +O(h^2)\\ \varphi_{\alpha,2} &=&(b_0-\f{a_0}{2} h D_2^0)\varphi_0 +h(a_0 b_0 L_+^{-1}[1]-a_0 L_-^{-1}[b_0-\alpha_0 \varphi_0]) +O(h^2), \end{eqnarray*} which is the final claim in Theorem \ref{102}.
nodes.section: 3.2 Solutions of 3.2 - rigorous construction
nodes.statement_short: Read off d^0 and recover the expansions (1.14)-(1.15).

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2, part 1: modulational eigenvalue of M_h
nodes.statement: We set up the following ansatz for the eigenvalue problem for $\mathcal M_h$, \begin{equation} \mathcal M_h \left(\begin{array}{c} h p_1 \\ \varphi_0 + h p_2 \end{array}\right)=\sigma h \left(\begin{array}{c} h p_1 \\ \varphi_0+ h p_2 \end{array}\right). \end{equation} Using the precise form of $\mathcal M_h$, to the leading order $h$, we have \begin{eqnarray*} & & L_+ p_1 + 2 \varphi_0^2 (2 b_0 \Psi_1^0-2 a_0 \Psi_2^0-D_2^0)=0 \\ & & L_- p_2 -4\varphi_0^2(a_0\Psi_1^0+b_0 \Psi_2^0)=\sigma \varphi_0 \end{eqnarray*} The first equation is resolvable, since $ 2 \varphi_0^2 (2 b_0 \Psi_1^0-2 a_0 \Psi_2^0-D_2^0)$ is even and hence perpendicular to $Ker[L_+]=span[\varphi_0']$. The solvability condition for the second one, $\sigma \varphi_0 + 4\varphi_0^2(a_0\Psi_1^0+b_0 \Psi_2^0)\perp \varphi_0$, is what yields the formula for $\sigma_0$, namely \begin{equation} \sigma_0=-4\f{\dpr{\varphi_0^2(a_0\Psi_1^0+b_0 \Psi_2^0)}{\varphi_0}}{\|\varphi_0\|^2}= -4 a_0\f{\dpr{L_+^{-1}[1]}{\varphi_0^3}}{\|\varphi_0\|^2}=a_0\f{\dpr{1}{\varphi_0}}{\|\varphi_0\|^2}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 4.1 Tracking the modulational eigenvalue for ${\mathcal L}_h$ $0<h<<1$
nodes.statement_short: Perturbative ansatz for the modulational kernel vector of M_h; the solvability condition gives its first-order shift sigma_0.

nodes.name: Ansatz
nodes.statement: We set up the following ansatz for the eigenvalue problem for $\mathcal M_h$, \begin{equation} \mathcal M_h \left(\begin{array}{c} h p_1 \\ \varphi_0 + h p_2 \end{array}\right)=\sigma h \left(\begin{array}{c} h p_1 \\ \varphi_0+ h p_2 \end{array}\right). \end{equation}
nodes.section: 4.1 Tracking the modulational eigenvalue for ${\mathcal L}_h$ $0<h<<1$
nodes.statement_short: Eigenvector (hp_1, phi_0+hp_2) with eigenvalue sigma h.

nodes.name: Leading order
nodes.statement: Using the precise form of $\mathcal M_h$, to the leading order $h$, we have \begin{eqnarray*} & & L_+ p_1 + 2 \varphi_0^2 (2 b_0 \Psi_1^0-2 a_0 \Psi_2^0-D_2^0)=0 \\ & & L_- p_2 -4\varphi_0^2(a_0\Psi_1^0+b_0 \Psi_2^0)=\sigma \varphi_0 \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.section: 4.1 Tracking the modulational eigenvalue for ${\mathcal L}_h$ $0<h<<1$
nodes.statement_short: First-order equations for p_1, p_2.

nodes.name: Solve for p_1
nodes.statement: The first equation is resolvable, since $ 2 \varphi_0^2 (2 b_0 \Psi_1^0-2 a_0 \Psi_2^0-D_2^0)$ is even and hence perpendicular to $Ker[L_+]=span[\varphi_0']$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Tracking the modulational eigenvalue for ${\mathcal L}_h$ $0<h<<1$
nodes.statement_short: Even right-hand side is orthogonal to Ker L_+.

nodes.name: Formula for sigma_0
nodes.statement: The solvability condition for the second one, $\sigma \varphi_0 + 4\varphi_0^2(a_0\Psi_1^0+b_0 \Psi_2^0)\perp \varphi_0$, is what yields the formula for $\sigma_0$, namely \begin{equation} \sigma_0=-4\f{\dpr{\varphi_0^2(a_0\Psi_1^0+b_0 \Psi_2^0)}{\varphi_0}}{\|\varphi_0\|^2}= -4 a_0\f{\dpr{L_+^{-1}[1]}{\varphi_0^3}}{\|\varphi_0\|^2}=a_0\f{\dpr{1}{\varphi_0}}{\|\varphi_0\|^2}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 4.1 Tracking the modulational eigenvalue for ${\mathcal L}_h$ $0<h<<1$
nodes.statement_short: Solvability gives sigma_0=a_0<1,phi_0>/||phi_0||^2.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2, part 2: modulational eigenvalue of J L_h
nodes.statement: Taking cues from the proof of Proposition \ref{prop:11}, we take the following ansatz for the (former) modulation eigenvalue at zero and the corresponding eigenvector $\left(\begin{array}{c} 0 \\ \varphi_0 \end{array}\right)$ - take $\mu=\mu_0 \sqrt{h}$ and $\left(\begin{array}{c} Z_1 \\ Z_2 \end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}{c} \sqrt{h} q_1 \\ \varphi_0+h q_2 \end{array}\right)$. Plugging this in \eqref{570}, we obtain, after some elementary algebraic manipulations, \begin{eqnarray*} \left(\begin{array}{cc} L_+ +O(h) & O(h) \\ O(h) & L_- - 4 h \varphi_0 (a_0 \Psi_1^0+b_0 \Psi_2^0) \end{array} \right) \left(\begin{array}{c} \sqrt{h} q_1 \\ \varphi_0+h q_2 \end{array}\right)=\mu_0 \sqrt{h} \left(\begin{array}{c} -\varphi_0-h q_2 \\ \sqrt{h} q_1 \end{array} \right) \end{eqnarray*} Resolving the first equation, to its leading order $\sqrt{h}$, yields the relation $ L_+ q_1 = -\mu_0 \varphi_0, $ or, since $L_+$ is invertible on $\varphi_0$, \begin{equation} q_1=-\mu_0 L_+^{-1}[\varphi_0]+O(\sqrt{h}). \end{equation} In the second equation, the leading order is $h$, whence we get the equation \begin{equation} L_- q_2 - 4 \varphi_0^2(a_0 \Psi_1^0+b_0 \Psi_2^0) = \mu_0 q_1= -\mu_0^2 L_+^{-1}[\varphi_0]. \end{equation} This equation is solvable, provided we ensure $4 \varphi_0^2(a_0 \Psi_1^0+b_0 \Psi_2^0) - \mu_0^2 L_+^{-1}[\varphi_0]\perp \varphi_0$, as the operator $L_-$ becomes invertible on it, whence $$ q_2=L_-^{-1}[4 \varphi_0^2(a_0 \Psi_1^0+b_0 \Psi_2^0) - \mu_0^2 L_+^{-1}[\varphi_0]]. $$ Thus, we have located the former modulational invariance eigenvalue - namely it is $\mu_0 \sqrt{h}$, where $\mu_0$ ensures $4 \varphi_0^2(a_0 \Psi_1^0+b_0 \Psi_2^0) - \mu_0^2 L_+^{-1}[\varphi_0]\perp \varphi_0$. Equivalently \begin{equation} \mu_0^2 = 4 \f{\dpr{\varphi_0^2(a_0 \Psi_1^0+b_0 \Psi_2^0)}{\varphi_0}}{\dpr{L_+^{-1}\varphi_0}{\varphi_0}}. \end{equation} It remains to compute this last expression. We have \begin{eqnarray*} \mu_0^2 &=& 4\f{\dpr{\varphi_0^3}{a_0 \Psi_1^0+b_0 \Psi_2^0}}{\dpr{L_+^{-1}\varphi_0}{\varphi_0}}= 4 \f{a_0}{ \dpr{L_+^{-1}\varphi_0}{\varphi_0}} \dpr{\varphi_0^3}{L_+^{-1}[1]}= -a_0 \f{\dpr{\varphi_0}{1}}{\dpr{L_+^{-1}\varphi_0}{\varphi_0}} \end{eqnarray*} Since $\dpr{L_+^{-1}\varphi_0}{\varphi_0}<0$, we have that $sgn(\mu_0^2)=sgn(a_0)$. In other words, if $a_0>0$, we have instability, while for $a_0<0$, we have a marginally stable pairs of eigenvalues $\pm i [\sqrt \f{-a_0 \dpr{\varphi_0}{1}}{\dpr{L_+^{-1}\varphi_0}{\varphi_0}} \sqrt{h}+O(h)]$
nodes.section: 4.2 Tracking the modulational eigenvalue for ${\mathcal J} {\mathcal L}_h$ $0<h<<1$
nodes.statement_short: Ansatz mu=mu_0 sqrt(h) as in Proposition 5; solvability at order h gives mu_0^2 = -a_0<phi_0,1>/<L_+^{-1}phi_0,phi_0>, so sign(mu_0^2)=sign(a_0).

nodes.name: Ansatz
nodes.statement: Taking cues from the proof of Proposition \ref{prop:11}, we take the following ansatz for the (former) modulation eigenvalue at zero and the corresponding eigenvector $\left(\begin{array}{c} 0 \\ \varphi_0 \end{array}\right)$ - take $\mu=\mu_0 \sqrt{h}$ and $\left(\begin{array}{c} Z_1 \\ Z_2 \end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}{c} \sqrt{h} q_1 \\ \varphi_0+h q_2 \end{array}\right)$.
nodes.section: 4.2 Tracking the modulational eigenvalue for ${\mathcal J} {\mathcal L}_h$ $0<h<<1$
nodes.statement_short: mu=mu_0 sqrt(h) with eigenvector (sqrt(h) q_1, phi_0+hq_2).

nodes.name: Substitute
nodes.statement: Plugging this in \eqref{570}, we obtain, after some elementary algebraic manipulations, \begin{eqnarray*} \left(\begin{array}{cc} L_+ +O(h) & O(h) \\ O(h) & L_- - 4 h \varphi_0 (a_0 \Psi_1^0+b_0 \Psi_2^0) \end{array} \right) \left(\begin{array}{c} \sqrt{h} q_1 \\ \varphi_0+h q_2 \end{array}\right)=\mu_0 \sqrt{h} \left(\begin{array}{c} -\varphi_0-h q_2 \\ \sqrt{h} q_1 \end{array} \right) \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.section: 4.2 Tracking the modulational eigenvalue for ${\mathcal J} {\mathcal L}_h$ $0<h<<1$
nodes.statement_short: Plug the ansatz into (4.3).

nodes.name: Solve for q_1
nodes.statement: Resolving the first equation, to its leading order $\sqrt{h}$, yields the relation $ L_+ q_1 = -\mu_0 \varphi_0, $ or, since $L_+$ is invertible on $\varphi_0$, \begin{equation} q_1=-\mu_0 L_+^{-1}[\varphi_0]+O(\sqrt{h}). \end{equation}
nodes.section: 4.2 Tracking the modulational eigenvalue for ${\mathcal J} {\mathcal L}_h$ $0<h<<1$
nodes.statement_short: q_1=-mu_0 L_+^{-1}phi_0 to leading order.

nodes.name: Equation for q_2
nodes.statement: In the second equation, the leading order is $h$, whence we get the equation \begin{equation} L_- q_2 - 4 \varphi_0^2(a_0 \Psi_1^0+b_0 \Psi_2^0) = \mu_0 q_1= -\mu_0^2 L_+^{-1}[\varphi_0]. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 4.2 Tracking the modulational eigenvalue for ${\mathcal J} {\mathcal L}_h$ $0<h<<1$
nodes.statement_short: Order-h equation for q_2.

nodes.name: Solvability
nodes.statement: This equation is solvable, provided we ensure $4 \varphi_0^2(a_0 \Psi_1^0+b_0 \Psi_2^0) - \mu_0^2 L_+^{-1}[\varphi_0]\perp \varphi_0$, as the operator $L_-$ becomes invertible on it, whence $$ q_2=L_-^{-1}[4 \varphi_0^2(a_0 \Psi_1^0+b_0 \Psi_2^0) - \mu_0^2 L_+^{-1}[\varphi_0]]. $$
nodes.section: 4.2 Tracking the modulational eigenvalue for ${\mathcal J} {\mathcal L}_h$ $0<h<<1$
nodes.statement_short: Solvability condition and q_2.

nodes.name: Formula for mu_0^2
nodes.statement: Thus, we have located the former modulational invariance eigenvalue - namely it is $\mu_0 \sqrt{h}$, where $\mu_0$ ensures $4 \varphi_0^2(a_0 \Psi_1^0+b_0 \Psi_2^0) - \mu_0^2 L_+^{-1}[\varphi_0]\perp \varphi_0$. Equivalently \begin{equation} \mu_0^2 = 4 \f{\dpr{\varphi_0^2(a_0 \Psi_1^0+b_0 \Psi_2^0)}{\varphi_0}}{\dpr{L_+^{-1}\varphi_0}{\varphi_0}}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 4.2 Tracking the modulational eigenvalue for ${\mathcal J} {\mathcal L}_h$ $0<h<<1$
nodes.statement_short: The eigenvalue is mu_0 sqrt(h) with mu_0^2 given by (4.8).

nodes.name: Compute mu_0^2
nodes.statement: It remains to compute this last expression. We have \begin{eqnarray*} \mu_0^2 &=& 4\f{\dpr{\varphi_0^3}{a_0 \Psi_1^0+b_0 \Psi_2^0}}{\dpr{L_+^{-1}\varphi_0}{\varphi_0}}= 4 \f{a_0}{ \dpr{L_+^{-1}\varphi_0}{\varphi_0}} \dpr{\varphi_0^3}{L_+^{-1}[1]}= -a_0 \f{\dpr{\varphi_0}{1}}{\dpr{L_+^{-1}\varphi_0}{\varphi_0}} \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.section: 4.2 Tracking the modulational eigenvalue for ${\mathcal J} {\mathcal L}_h$ $0<h<<1$
nodes.statement_short: Evaluate using L_+^{-1}[phi_0^3]=-phi_0/4.

nodes.name: Sign dichotomy
nodes.statement: Since $\dpr{L_+^{-1}\varphi_0}{\varphi_0}<0$, we have that $sgn(\mu_0^2)=sgn(a_0)$. nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2, part 4: even subspace
nodes.statement: In this case, we have established the emergence, from the modulational eigenvalue at $h=0$ (which has algebraic multiplicity two!), of a pair of marginally stable eigenvalues $i [\pm \mu_0 \sqrt{h}+O(h)]$. We now compute the Krein index of the marginally stable pair of eigenvalues\footnote{which is of course relevant computation, only if $b_0>a_0$.} $ \pm i \sqrt{\mu_0} \sqrt{h} +O(h)$ For a simple pair of eigenvalues, the Krein index coincides with the sign of the expression $\dpr{ \Re \left(\begin{array}{c} \sqrt{h} q_1 \\ \varphi_0+h q_2 \end{array}\right)}{ \mathcal M_h \Re \left(\begin{array}{c} \sqrt{h} q_1 \\ \varphi_0+h q_2 \end{array}\right)}$, see \cite{KKS}, p. 267. To this end, realizing from \eqref{598} that $q_1$ is purely imaginary to the leading order (in the case under consideration), \begin{eqnarray*} & & \dpr{ \Re \left(\begin{array}{c} \sqrt{h} q_1 \\ \varphi_0+h q_2 \end{array}\right)}{ \mathcal M_h \Re \left(\begin{array}{c} \sqrt{h} q_1 \\ \varphi_0+h q_2 \end{array}\right)} = -4h \dpr{\varphi_0}{\varphi_0^2(a_0 \Psi_1^0+b_0\Psi_2^0)}+O(h^{3/2})= \\ &=& -4 a_0 h \dpr{\varphi_0^3}{L_+^{-1}[1]}+O(h^{3/2})= a_0 h \dpr{\varphi_0}{1}+O(h^{3/2}). \end{eqnarray*} It follows that for $a_0<0$, the problem has a pair of eigenvalues $ \pm i \sqrt{\mu_0} \sqrt{h} +O(h)$ with a negative Krein signature. Recall that $n({\mathcal L}_0)=1$, which arises in the even subspace. Moreover, $dim(Ker[{\mathcal L}_0])=2$, but recall that one of them occurs in the even subspace, the other one in the odd subspace. On the other hand\footnote{For a self-adjoint, bounded from below operator $M$, acting invariantly on the even subspace, we denote $n_{even}(M)$ the number of negative eigenvalues, when acting on the even subspace} $n_{even}({\mathcal L}_h)$ could assume the values of one or two - $n_{even}({\mathcal L}_h)=1$, if the translational eigenvalue \eqref{b:50} is positive or $n_{even}({\mathcal L}_h)=2$, if the modulational eigenvalue \eqref{b:50} is negative. Indeed, ${\mathcal L}_{0, even}$ has one negative eigenvalue, according to Proposition \ref{prop:h0} - which remains negative, after the perturbation. In addition, the modulational eigenvalue at zero has moved (for $a_0<0$) to the left, see \eqref{b:90}, creating a second negative eigenvalue. We claim that $n({\mathcal L}_h)=2$, at least for small $0<h<<1$. Indeed, since by the index counting formulas $$ 0\leq n_{unstable, even}({\mathcal J} {\mathcal L}_h)\leq n({\mathcal L}_h)-\# \{\lambda\in i \mathbf R: \lambda \ \ \textup{has negative Krein signature} \}\leq n_{even}({\mathcal L}_h)-2\leq 0. $$ since we have already verified that there is at least one pair of purely imaginary eigenvalues, $\pm i \sqrt{\mu_0} \sqrt{h} +O(h)$ with negative Krein signatures (and even eigenfunctions!). Thus, we obtain equalities everywhere in the inequalities above, in particular $n_{unstable, even }({\mathcal J} {\mathcal L}_h)=0$, \\ $n({\mathcal L}_{h, even})=2$. In other words, the modulational eigenvalue has moved to the left (for $a_0<0$), creating a total of two negative eigenvalue for ${\mathcal L}_h$ - one that existed for ${\mathcal L}_0$ (and it is still there, after the perturbation), to which another one is added. These are subsequently offset by two purely imaginary eigenvalues, with negative Krein signatures.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2, part 5: odd subspace and conclusion
nodes.statement: For the odd subspace, the index count is somewhat simpler. Recall there is the ``unstable'' eigenvalue at $\mu=\alpha=\alpha_0 h$ for the eigenvalue problem \eqref{570}, which corresponds to the translational invariance, see \eqref{550} and the discussion immediately after. So, this implies that $n_{unstable, odd}({\mathcal J} {\mathcal L}_h)\geq 1$. On the other hand, $n_{odd}(L_+)\leq 1$, since the translational eigenvalue has moved either to the left (in which case $n_{odd}(L_+)=1$), or to the right, and then\footnote{See the Appendix for a calculation involving the direction of the move, which turns out to be inconclusive to first order} $n_{odd}(L_+)=0$. Applying the index counting theory, we have that on the other hand $n_{odd}(L_+)\geq n_{unstable,odd}({\mathcal J} {\mathcal L}_h)$, whence $1=n_{unstable, odd}({\mathcal J} {\mathcal L}_h)=n_{odd}(L_+)$. In particular, the translational eigenvalue has moved to the left to become a negative eigenvalue for ${\mathcal L}_{+,h}$. In addition, the ``unstable eigenvalue'' is exactly the one computed explicitly, namely $\mu=\alpha$ and there are no other unstable eigenvalues in the odd subspace. Note that by the Hamiltonian symmetry the eigenvalues of \eqref{570}are symmetric with respect to the imaginary axes, so there is another, stable one at $\mu=-\alpha$. We mention that there could be (and there is!) a lot of (point) spectrum on the imaginary axes as well. In terms of the original spectral variables, by combining the conclusions for the even and odd subspaces, we obtain $$ \lambda=\mu-\alpha\subset \left\{\{\alpha\}\cup\{-\alpha\} \cup \{\lambda: \Re \lambda=0\} \right\} - \alpha = \{0\}\cup\{-2\alpha\} \cup \{\lambda: \Re \lambda=-\alpha\}. $$ This is exactly the statement of Theorem \ref{105} and the proof is completed.

nodes.name: Derivation of the first-order translational eigenvalue
nodes.statement: We set up the following ansatz for the eigenvalue problem for $\mathcal M_h$, \begin{equation} \mathcal M_h \left(\begin{array}{c} \varphi_0'+h p_1 \\ h p_2 \end{array}\right)=\sigma h \left(\begin{array}{c} \varphi_0'+h p_1 \\ h p_2 \end{array}\right). \end{equation} In other words, \begin{equation} \left(\begin{array}{cc} L_+ - 12 h \varphi_0 (a_0 \Psi_1^0+b_0 \Psi_2^0) & O(h) \\ 2h \varphi_0(2 b_0\Psi_1^0-2 a_0 \Psi_2^0-D_2^0)& L_-+O(h) \end{array}\right) \left(\begin{array}{c} \varphi_0'+h p_1 \\ h p_2 \end{array}\right)=\sigma h \left(\begin{array}{c} \varphi_0' +h p_1 \\ h p_2 \end{array}\right). \end{equation} To the leading order $h$, we have the equations \begin{eqnarray*} & & L_+ p_1 - 12 \varphi_0 (a_0 \Psi_1^0+b_0 \Psi_2^0) \varphi_0'=\sigma \varphi_0' \\ & & L_- p_2 + 2 \varphi_0(2 b_0\Psi_1^0 - 2 a_0 \Psi_2^0-D_2^0) \varphi_0'=0 \end{eqnarray*} The second equation always has a solution as $2 \varphi_0(2 b_0\Psi_1^0 - 2 a_0 \Psi_2^0-D_2^0) \varphi_0'$ is an odd function, so it is perpendicular to $Ker[L_-]=span[\varphi_0]$. The first equation requires the solvability condition $\sigma \varphi_0' + 12 \varphi_0 (a_0 \Psi_1^0+b_0 \Psi_2^0) \varphi_0'\perp \varphi_0'$. Noting that $a_0 \Psi_1^0+b_0 \Psi_2^0=a_0 L_+^{-1}[1]$, we derive the formula for $\sigma_0$, \begin{equation} \sigma_0=-12 \f{\dpr{\varphi_0 \varphi_0'(a_0 \Psi_1^0+b_0 \Psi_2^0)}{\varphi_0'}}{\|\varphi_0'\|^2}= -12 \f{a_0}{\|\varphi_0'\|^2} \dpr{ L_{+}^{-1}[1]}{\varphi_0 (\varphi_0')^2}. \end{equation} This quantity can be computed explicitly, in fact $\dpr{ L_{+}^{-1}[1]}{\varphi_0 (\varphi_0')^2}=0$, see Proposition \ref{antany} below.

that $\varphi_0''(T)=\alpha^3\kappa^2\sqrt{1-\kappa^2}$, and $\psi'(T)=\sqrt{1-\kappa^2}\int_{0}^{T}{\frac{1-2sn^2(\alpha x)}{dn^2(\alpha x)}}dx$, we get $$ nodes.name: Proof of (B.1)
nodes.statement: For the proof of \eqref{ant1}, recall the basic properties at $h=0$. In this case the equation (\ref{1.2}) has a solution $$\varphi_0(x)=\alpha dn (\alpha x, \kappa), $$ where $\kappa^2=\frac{2\alpha^2-1}{\alpha^2}$. Also $L_+=-\partial_x^2+1-2(\varphi_0)^2$. Since $L_+\varphi_0'=0$, the function $$\psi(x)=\varphi_0'(x)\int^{x}{\frac{1}{\varphi_0'^2(s)}}ds, \; \; \left| \begin{array}{cc} \varphi_0'& \psi \\ \varphi_0'' & \psi'\end{array}\right|=1 $$ is also solution of $L_+\psi=0$. Formally, since $\varphi_0'$ has zeros using the identities $$\frac{1}{cn^2(y,\kappa)}=\frac{1}{dn(y, \kappa)}\frac{\partial}{\partial_y}\frac{sn(x, \kappa)}{cn(y, \kappa)}, \; \; \frac{1}{sn^2(y,\kappa)}=-\frac{1}{dn(y, \kappa)}\frac{\partial}{\partial_y}\frac{cn(x, \kappa)}{sn(y, \kappa)}$$ and integrating by parts we get $$ \psi(x) =\frac{1}{\alpha^2\kappa^2}\left[\frac{1-2sn^2(\alpha x, \kappa )}{dn (\alpha x, \kappa) } - \alpha \kappa^2sn(\alpha x, \kappa)cn(\alpha x, \kappa) \int_{0}^{x}{\frac{1-2sn^2(\alpha s, \kappa )}{dn^2(\alpha s, \kappa)}}ds\right] $$ Thus, we may construct Green function $$L_+^{-1}f=\varphi_0'\int_{0}^{x}{\psi(s)f(s)}ds-\psi(s)\int_{0}^{x}{\varphi_0'(s)f(s)}s+C_f\psi(x), $$ where $C_f$ is chosen such that $L_{+,0}^{-1}f$ is periodic with same period as $\varphi_0(x)$. After integrating by parts, we get \begin{equation} \langle L_+^{-1}\varphi_0, \varphi_0\rangle = -\langle \varphi_0^3, \psi \rangle +\frac{\varphi_0^2(T)+\varphi_0^2}{2}\langle \varphi_0, \psi \rangle +C_{\varphi_0}\langle \varphi_0, \psi \rangle, \end{equation} We have \begin{equation} \begin{array}{ll} \langle \varphi_0, \psi \rangle =\frac{1}{\alpha^2 \kappa^2}[E(\kappa)-K(\kappa)] \\ \\ \langle \varphi_0^3, \psi \rangle =\frac{1}{2\kappa^2} [(2-\kappa^2)E(\kappa)-2(1-\kappa^2)K(\kappa)] \\ \\ C_{\varphi_0}=-\frac{\varphi_0''(T)}{2\psi(T)}\langle \varphi_0, \psi \rangle+\frac{\varphi_0^2(T)-\varphi_0^2(0)}{2}. \end{array} \end{equation} With this finally we get $$\dpr{L_+^{-1} \varphi_0} {\varphi_0} = \frac{E^2(\kappa)-(1-\kappa^2)K^2(\kappa)}{2[2(1-\kappa^2)K(\kappa)-(2-\kappa^2)E(\kappa)]}<0. $$ see Figure \ref{fig1} below. \begin{figure}[h] \centering \includegraphics[width=8cm,height=6cm]{grafika_1.pdf} \caption{The function $k\to\frac{E^2(\kappa)-(1-\kappa^2)K^2(\kappa)}{2[2(1-\kappa^2)K(\kappa)-(2-\kappa^2)E(\kappa)]}$ } \end{figure}
